messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 54, Daniel had spent most of his adult life trying to live by order, procedure, and restraint, which made what happened to him on a winter night still feel, in his telling, like a violation not only of his body but of everything he believed the job stood for. He was working as a parole officer in a cramped county office on the edge of town when he was taken aside during a routine transport by officers he knew from years of coordination with local law enforcement. A disagreement about a client’s behavior escalated in front of him, and he watched police use force that, in his view, went far beyond any need for control. He remembered the flash of a hallway light, the echo of raised voices, then the hard impact of being shoved and pinned while someone he had trusted as a professional ally acted with a cruelty that left him stunned. From that night on, Daniel came to believe he had been betrayed by someone he trusted, that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it, and that the very people and institutions meant to protect him had let him down. Those beliefs settled quickly into his account of the event; he could not think about it without moving back and forth between anger and a kind of stunned disbelief, as though the details themselves were intolerable and proof of a larger injustice.

In the weeks that followed, ordinary moments at work began to carry a charge they had not had before. If a supervisee arrived late, spoke back, or acted disrespectfully, Daniel felt a flash of heat and a tightening in his chest, as if misbehavior itself announced that something dangerous was underway. He had come to read stress in the office as a warning sign, and when his own heart started racing during a tense meeting or after a difficult phone call, it confirmed for him that he was not simply uneasy but that danger might be near. That bodily alarm made him think again of betrayal and unfairness, and it sharpened his sense that he had been left unprotected; at the same time, it made any unruly behavior feel bigger, less containable, and more personally threatening than it might have once seemed. He began to scan his surroundings constantly for signs of danger, watching doorways, hands, tone of voice, and the mood in a room before he could fully register what was happening. Unusual silence was especially hard for him. If a hallway at the office went quiet or a room fell still, he felt something dangerous was about to happen, and that silence could pull him back toward the memory he tried not to fully recall. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could complete it, because once it came close, it felt so extreme that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him; the event existed in his mind as an incomplete picture, with certain fragments vivid and the rest missing, as though the mind had broken away from it to protect itself. Yet the fragments he could not fully hold onto—boots on tile, the force of being controlled, the sense of humiliation—were enough to keep the injustice alive, and the more he tried to suppress the memory, the more his body and thoughts seemed to circle back to the same conclusion that he had been wronged and abandoned.

Over months, Daniel’s life narrowed around that loop. On his commute he avoided traffic jams and anything that made him feel trapped; at work he kept conversations brief, stood near exits, and preferred to review files alone rather than stay in rooms where silence might suddenly fall. His wife noticed that he became jumpy at home, too, startling when a refrigerator door slammed or when the house went quiet at night. Even when he tried to rest, his attention drifted outward, scanning, waiting, and the work of staying alert made him feel as if the danger had never really ended. What troubled him most was that the same bodily surge, the same racing heart, could send him back into the story of being betrayed, unfairly treated, and failed by the institutions around him. At those moments, people misbehaving at work or on the street no longer looked merely rude or difficult; they looked like evidence that the world remained hostile and that he could still be caught off guard. The memory, always partial and half-repulsed, fed the sense that something had been covered over or left unresolved, and that unresolved quality fed his outrage and his watchfulness in turn. He became more certain that he could not trust silence, authority, or his own body when it warned him.

By the time he finally sought help, Daniel was no longer able to dismiss the pattern as stress from a demanding job. He came in after a week in which a young supervisee’s defiance at the office set off his heart racing, made him scan the room for danger, and left him preoccupied with the old sense of being betrayed all day. At home he had begun to dread quiet evenings, because the silence in the house seemed to press the memory toward him again, fragments and all, and he no longer wanted his wife to see how quickly he was startled. He was hoping, cautiously, to make sense of why these moments still hit so hard and to regain some confidence that he could do his work without feeling constantly on guard. What he feared most was that the same unfairness and abandonment would keep repeating itself—that he would stay trapped between the half-remembered event and the certainty that, once again, no one would protect him.
